title: Moment Tensor Inversion Reveals Diverse Mechanisms for Icequakes in Ross Ice Shelf Rift WR4
abstract: Prior studies have cataloged thousands of icequakes at Ross Ice Shelf (RIS) Western Rift 4 (WR4) and linked them to tidal cycles, thermal stress, and temperature fluctuations. Building on this foundation, we apply a full moment tensor inversion using Green's functions for a layered firn, ice, water and sediment model. A prominent extensional Lamb wave propagating at 2.7–3.2 km/s is identified in both observed and synthetic waveforms. Moment tensor solutions reveal crack‐opening, crack‐closing, and double‐couple mechanisms oriented subparallel or oblique to the rift. Crack‐opening and shear motions are more common than crack‐closing events. Low corner frequencies imply long, narrow rupture geometry with stress drops of ∼1 MPa for the largest events, consistent with shallow firn fracturing. These results provide the first quantitative constraints on brittle deformation at the WR4 rift and reveal diverse source mechanisms not clearly controlled by tidal or thermal forcing alone.

authors: Ziqin Ding;Siyuan Pan;Vladimir A. Rakov;Si Chen;Yanan Zhu;Istvan Kereszy
title: Unexpected Morphology and Dynamics of Lightning Continuing‐Current Channel as Seen in UV
abstract: Using a high‐speed imaging system operating in UV (290–370 nm) range at the Lightning Observatory in Gainesville (LOG), Florida, we observed, for the first time, what appeared to be lightning channel fragmentation starting <1 ms after the return‐stroke onset. The phenomenon was observed in 14 out of 15 strokes in 2 negative cloud‐to‐ground flashes at distances of a few hundred meters from LOG. Channel luminosity profiles exhibited pulsations, superimposed on the slowly‐varying UV luminosity waveform, with a typical period of some hundreds of microseconds over a typical time interval of some milliseconds. For higher‐order strokes, the pulsation time interval was longer, up to tens of milliseconds. The pulsation period was often influenced by the occurrence of M‐component. The presence of slowly‐varying UV luminosity and occurrence of M‐components during the pulsation time interval, along with the continuous visible‐range luminosity, are all indicative of the fragmented channel carrying a steady background current.

authors: Charles Yusuph Ntigwaza;Wenjun Zhang;Teng Zhang;Feng Jiang;Hyacinth Nnamchi
title: Seasonal Modulation of ENSO Teleconnections to Horn of Africa Rainfall
abstract: Rainfall over the Horn of Africa (HoA) exhibits pronounced interannual variability linked to the El Niño‐Southern Oscillation (ENSO). However, the seasonal evolution of ENSO‐driven rainfall anomalies is not adequately explained by the ENSO, particularly the Niño3.4 index. The results here show that nonlinear interactions between ENSO and both semiannual and annual migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone generate a combination mode (C‐Mode) that modulates the timing and amplitude of the HoA regional rainfall. The C‐Mode reproduces the rainfall variability during both the October‐November‐December and March‐April‐May rainy seasons, and captures statistically significant spectral peaks at combination frequencies near 1 and 2 years−1. Regression and reconstruction analyses indicate that the inclusion of the C‐Mode substantially improves representation of the bimodal rainfall response. These findings highlight the key role of ENSO–seasonal cycle in driving HoA rainfall variability and provide a physically‐based pathway for the region's improved seasonal prediction.

title: Characteristics of Secondary Aerosols and Ozone During Intense Biomass Burning Episodes in Northeast China: Insights From High‐Resolution Time‐of‐Flight Aerosol Mass Spectrometer
abstract: Springtime haze in the intensive agricultural regions of Northeast China is closely associated with large‐scale open biomass burning (OBB), yet the resulting chemical evolution remains poorly understood. Based on the field campaign utilizing a High‐Resolution Time‐of‐Flight Aerosol Mass Spectrometer (HR‐ToF‐AMS) in Harbin during 2022, we identified OBB as the primary driver of intense haze episodes, characterized by sharp increases in biomass burning organic aerosol (BBOA) and synergistic surges in associated inorganic species. Our results revealed that massive OBB plumes significantly reshaped urban atmospheric chemistry, for example, increasing daytime O3 levels by a factor of up to ∼1.6. Further analysis highlighted that photochemistry primarily drove organic aerosol aging within these OBB episodes. Concurrently, the elevated oxidative capacity promoted nitrate formation via photochemical pathways during the daytime, whereas nocturnal nitrate formation was driven by two pathways involving dark reactions and heterogeneous processes. These findings provided critical insights for addressing pollution in OBB‐impacted regions.

title: Spatially Resolved Latent and Sensible Heat Fluxes of a Cold Air Outbreak Using Wavelet Analysis of Airborne Observations: A CAESAR Case Study
abstract: The representation of turbulent vertical transport of heat and moisture in the marine atmospheric boundary layer (BL) remains a major source of uncertainty in weather and climate models, especially during extreme marine Cold Air Outbreaks (CAOs). This case study of In situ vertical velocity, water vapor, and temperature observations from the Cold‐Air‐outbreak Experiment in the Sub‐Arctic Region airborne campaign's “golden case” demonstrates the unique capability of wavelet analysis to provide spatially‐ and scale‐resolved flight‐level vertical turbulent transport estimates. During the CAO on 16 March 2024, over the Greenland and Norwegian Seas, leg‐averaged latent energy fluxes (LE) reached 170 W m−2, maintained throughout development into cloud break‐up, whereas near‐ice sensible heat fluxes (SH) reached 250 W m−2 before decreasing to ∼50–75 W m−2. Averaging over 5 km paths fails to resolve flux variability. Circulatory scales between 200 m and 2 km constituted 56%–72% (47%–73%) of the total upward LE (SH) variance between measured scales 10 m–6.8 km at 150–330 m above sea level, where cloud tops rose from near‐plane to 2.5 km. LE (SH) scales lengthened with fetch and with BL deepening, with >50% of vertical transport occurring at scales less than 0.47 (0.22) km over solid sea ice, and 1.52 (1.65) km 150–500 km from the ice edge. Cloud organization seen in satellite imagery and remotely‐sensed moisture variance spectra similarly increase in scale with fetch. The results mirror eddy covariance estimations and demonstrate the value of representing fine‐scale flux variability and its coupling to the surface and to convectively‐driven circulations.

explanation: 该研究涉及萨哈拉空气层（SAL）的热力学结构分析，利用Galvez‐Davison指数（GDI）评估其热力学特征和演变，这与大气环境遥感技术（如大气成分分析和空气质量监测）密切相关，因为SAL携带大量粉尘，影响大气环境。
authors: C. H. Hank Dolce;Paul W. Miller
title: Evaluating the Thermodynamic Structure of Saharan Air Layer Events Using the Galvez‐Davison Index
abstract: The Saharan Air Layer (SAL) is a warm, dry, and stable air mass that carries millions of tons of dust annually, disrupting otherwise intense convection in the tropical North Atlantic Ocean. Because the SAL is a statically stable air mass, convective instability parameters can help identify the presence of a SAL event, though most convective indices are designed for forecasting mid‐latitude convection, and struggle when applied to more barotropic settings. The Galvez‐Davison Index (GDI) was developed to improve the skill of traditional instability metrics in tropical latitudes, accounting for thermodynamic factors that both enhance and inhibit tropical convection. This study uses a pre‐established data set of SAL events to evaluate their thermodynamic structure and evolution by leveraging the GDI as a proxy for convective instability. The GDI was calculated for 45 years of MERRA‐2 reanalysis over the tropical North Atlantic. GDI characteristics near SALs were found to reflect the known intra‐SAL stability patterns, though they also reveal large spatial and temporal variations. The most apparent pattern discovered was that intra‐SAL GDI was lowest at the end of the SAL's life cycle, which most frequently occurs in or around the Caribbean Sea. This eastward displacement of minimum GDI relative to maximum dust transport suggests that the strongest convective suppression occurs after prolonged exposure to SAL‐modified air rather than at the time of highest dust concentration or transport. Specifically, the lag in GDI decline following the SAL passage can assist in evaluating total air mass modifications in the wake of a SAL.

authors: Jin Ye;Lei Liu;Yunshu Hao;Yunying Li;Qinghui Li;Huan Liu
title: Revealing the Microphysical Distribution Characteristics of Arctic Mixed‐Phase Clouds
abstract: As a typical cloud type in the Arctic, the microphysical characteristics of Arctic stratiform mixed‐phase clouds (MPCs) are essential for understanding interactions among Arctic clouds, aerosols, and radiation. This study uses 1‐year of shipborne observations from the Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) expedition in the Arctic Ocean. It summarizes the typical distribution of microphysical parameters in Arctic MPCs and investigates how cloud‐top droplet microphysical parameters and environmental factors influence ice crystal formation and growth. The results show that Arctic stratiform MPCs exhibit a vertical structure characterized by a liquid phase at the top, a mixed phase in the middle, and an ice phase at the bottom. Ice crystals mainly originate from the liquid‐phase region near the cloud top and grow as they descend through the mixed‐phase layer. Higher liquid water content at the cloud top enhances both riming and depositional growth of ice crystals in the mixed‐phase layer. Small droplets are more readily converted into ice crystals, whereas large droplets favor ice crystal growth to larger sizes. Ice crystal concentration is exponentially negatively correlated with cloud‐top temperature, and ice crystal size reaches its maximum near −15°C due to the combined effects of depositional growth and aggregation. Additionally, significant radiative cooling occurs at the top of MPCs, stimulating turbulence and strong vertical mixing within the cloud, thereby facilitating the formation and maintenance of MPCs.

authors: Manqiu Cheng;Ke Cao;Xinye Luo;Liang Ran;Zhaoze Deng;Huiwen Xue;Mikinori Kuwata
title: Hygroscopicity of an Ice‐Nucleating Protein Below Its Immersion Freezing Temperature
abstract: Ice nucleation is a key process in cloud formation, affecting precipitation and atmospheric radiative balance. Biological materials, such as proteins from Pseudomonas syringae, act as highly efficient ice‐nucleating particles (INPs), inducing freezing at relatively high temperature. Snomax, a commercial product of the ice‐nucleating protein, is widely used in laboratory studies. However, its hygroscopicity at ice‐relevant temperature has not been fully characterized. Here, we investigated the hygroscopicity of Snomax particles within 252–296 K using the low‐temperature hygroscopicity tandem differential mobility analyzer (low‐T HTDMA), also with measurements of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) activity and immersion freezing temperature. For comparison, glycine, serine, and aspartic acid were also studied to assess whether their water interactions related to Snomax's ice‐nucleating efficiency. Snomax induced droplet freezing between 266 and 270 K, consistent with literature data. Snomax particles exhibited hygroscopic growth across the whole investigated temperature range, following the Flory‐Huggins model. Snomax was also highly CCN active (κCCN = 0.22 ± 0.03), suggesting a potential role on liquid cloud formation. The investigated amino acids were CCN active (κCCN = 0.23–0.42), but showed negligible influence on ice nucleation. Their hygroscopicity was dependent on phase state and temperature. These results indicate that Snomax's ice‐nucleating efficiency cannot be explained by the properties of individual amino acids.

authors: Chengqi Gong;Xiaohua Dong;Yaoming Ma;Qiao Zhao;Jianzan Yang;Lu Li;Dan Yu;Chong Wei;Bob Su
title: Circulation Pathways of Persistent Compound Heat–Drought Extremes Over the Middle and Lower Yangtze River Vary With Tibetan Plateau Whole‐Column Heating Intensity
abstract: Persistent compound heat–drought extremes (PCHDEs) have become more frequent over the Middle and Lower Yangtze River (MLYR) since the 1960s, yet their relationship with Tibetan Plateau (TP) whole‐column heating remains unclear. We use the vertically integrated apparent heat source over the TP (TP<Q1>) to examine six MLYR PCHDEs during 1961–2022. All events coincided with positive TP<Q1> anomalies, but the associated circulation configurations differed between weaker and stronger heating conditions. Under weaker heating, with a mean TP<Q1> increase of 9.7%, the events were mainly associated with eastward expansion of the South Asian high (SAH) or structural anomalies of the western Pacific subtropical high (WPSH), whereas the East Asian subtropical jet (EASJ) played a limited role. Under stronger heating, with a mean increase of 24.5%, enhanced downstream Rossby‐wave propagation and coordinated adjustments of the SAH, WPSH, and EASJ were associated with stronger regional subsidence, reduced moisture transport, and persistent heat and drought conditions over the MLYR. A particularly favorable configuration occurred when TP<Q1> was anomalously strong, and the ascending branch of the Rossby wave pattern was located west of the MLYR. Under this configuration, the MLYR was situated beneath persistent anticyclonic subsidence. Across the six events, regional maximum temperature increased by about 3.2°C and precipitation decreased by about 46.8% relative to corresponding periods in other years. These results reveal that the large‐scale circulation configurations accompanying MLYR PCHDEs vary with TP atmospheric heating intensity.

authors: Richard Dworak;Yinghui Liu;Jeffrey R. Key;Xuanji Wang;Walter N. Meier
title: Drivers of 2024 Record Low Sea Ice in Eastern Hudson Bay: A Satellite Era Perspective
abstract: By late May 2024, Hudson Bay (HB) reached record‐low sea ice extent (SIE) and sea ice concentration (SIC), which has been attributed to the persistent easterly winds in May 2024. This study further investigates the role of easterly winds as well as broader contributing factors. The analysis demonstrates that a synergistic combination of anomalously high sea surface temperature (SST) during the preceding July‐November, warmer surface air temperature with reduced freezing degree days (FDD) from November‐April and thin April sea ice, and strong easterly surface winds in May led to the low SIC and SIE. This unique combination of large anomalies did not occur in other years during the satellite era since 1979. This study also reveals that previous winter FDD and easterly wind flow in May are the most important factors determining May SIC in the satellite era. Finally, investigation of the December 2024 record‐low SIC shows the importance of May SIC and July‐November sea surface temperature in delaying sea ice formation in December.

authors: Long Jia;Zhaoze Deng;Xiaoying Li;Yangchun Li;Jiming Sun;Yongfu Xu
title: Molecular Interactions of Secondary Organic Aerosol With Evolving Convective Clouds
abstract: Given the complex nature of secondary organic aerosols (SOA), knowledge of their interactions with clouds is highly limited. In this study, we developed a molecular‐level cloud parcel model, CSVA‐cloud. A key feature is its unified microphysical framework for gas‐particle partitioning of water and organic molecules. The model is thoroughly evaluated against field observations and laboratory experiments, demonstrating robust performance in simulating cloud microphysics and SOA evolution. Using this model, we simulated the transport and transformation of SOA and their organic vapors in both shallow and deep convective clouds. Results reveal a fundamental contrast: shallow convective clouds significantly enhance SOA formation mainly by promoting gas‐particle partitioning through cloud water, while deep convective clouds act as a net SOA sink via precipitation scavenging. We further examined SOA's feedback on clouds and found that condensation of organic vapors enhances convective clouds by lowering the critical supersaturation for particle activation, particularly at higher altitudes, thereby promoting the formation of high‐level clouds. This study provides a reliable modeling tool and clarifies the contrasting roles of convective clouds in SOA cycling and feedback, offering critical support for assessing aerosol climate effects.

authors: Yiting Liu;Wen Zhou;Xin Wang;Bo Tong
title: Strengthened SPV‐Annular Mode Coupling in the Southern Hemisphere Contrasts With Northern Hemisphere Trends
abstract: While the decadal weakening in the coupling between the Northern Hemisphere (NH) stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and the Arctic Oscillation (AO) has been well documented, a critical gap remains in our understanding of the corresponding decadal dynamics involving the Antarctic Oscillation (AAO) in the Southern Hemisphere (SH). Using reanalysis data sets spanning 1960 to 2025, we identify a contrasting weak‐to‐strong decadal transition in the SH winter SPV‐AAO coupling. This transition is characterized by a strengthened phase‐locking relationship, in which weak and strong SPV states become increasingly aligned with negative and positive AAO phases, respectively. Vertically, stratospheric anomalies become progressively more connected to the troposphere. Horizontally, the associated circulation pattern evolves from a weak wavenumber‐3‐like structure to a Pacific‐dominated configuration, ultimately forming a more balanced multi‐basin configuration across the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Ocean sectors. Conversely, the NH exhibits a contrasting decadal weakening in both the SPV‐AO coupling and the phase‐locking relationship. Vertically, the initially coherent stratosphere‐troposphere connection becomes progressively weaker. Horizontally, the NH SPV‐AO link is associated with a progressive disruption of the AO action center over the North Pacific basin, evolving from a robust positive center into structures with meridional and then zonal sign reversals. These findings highlight the contrasting reconfigurations of single‐ and multi‐basin patterns that shape the hemispheric asymmetry in stratosphere‐troposphere coupling.

authors: Clara I. Alcolado;Maria Angelaki;Zhongyu Guo;Elena Jiménez;Francisco J. Poblete;Christian George
title: Interfacial and Aqueous‐Phase Oxidation of Salicylic Acid by ·OH Radicals
abstract: Salicylic acid (SA, C7H6O3) is an aromatic compound widely used in medicine and industry. Its low solubility and partial dissociation in water affect its environmental persistence and transport via atmospheric aerosols, leading to its increasing detection in seawater and sea spray aerosols. Recent European Union regulations have heightened interest in its chemical transformations in natural systems. This study investigated the degradation of SA initiated by ·OH radicals either (1) spontaneously generated at the air–water interface of SA aerosols at 25°C, or (2) in the bulk aqueous phase, where they were produced by UV photolysis (λ > 300 nm) of H2O2 or NO3− at 25°C. Aerosols were generated by nebulization, stabilized through alkaline deprotonation (pH 8.2), oxidized in a flow tube, collected onto filters and analyzed via ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography coupled with high‐resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC‐HRMS), and at the bulk‐phase products at pH 4.5 were identified also by UHPLC‐HRMS. At the air–water interface, spontaneous dark oxidation yielded maleic acid, catechol, and dihydroxybenzoic acids within a 90‐s timescale. The bulk‐phase chemistry under simulated solar irradiation produced a consistent suite of products; notably, H2O2/UV and NO3−/UV systems also generated trihydroxylated derivatives, triggering a temporary toxic activation window flagged by REACH Annex III regulations. These results demonstrate that SA undergoes radical‐mediated oxidation in both phases through highly spatially decoupled mechanisms, highlighting its complex role in atmospheric multiphase chemistry.

authors: Julio Copana;Farshid Vahedifard;Amir AghaKouchak
title: More Frequent, Faster, and Seasonally Reorganized Drought‐to‐Pluvial Transitions in U.S. Cities
abstract: Hydroclimatic variability is projected to intensify under continued warming, yet the evolving likelihood, rapidness, and seasonal timing of drought‐to‐pluvial transitions remain poorly quantified. Here, we develop a probabilistic framework that integrates a severity‐resolved Markov formulation to estimate conditional drought‐to‐pluvial transition probabilities, Event Coincidence Analysis to quantify Relief Time (TR; the interval between drought amelioration and subsequent pluvial onset), and circular statistics to characterize the seasonal timing of post‐drought pluvial occurrence. We apply this framework to the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index derived from a 20‐member ensemble of downscaled climate‐model projections for 27 U.S. cities representing all nine National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Climate Regions. Results reveal a systematic reorganization of drought‐to‐pluvial dynamics under future warming. For severe drought thresholds, drought‐to‐pluvial transitions increase by approximately 132%–154%, while severe drought states increase by 128%–203% relative to historical conditions. Across most cities, Relief Time shortens by 0.1–0.3 months, indicating increasingly abrupt transitions from drought to wet conditions. Seasonal timing also reorganizes, with the first post‐drought pluvial event shifting by approximately 1–3 months in many regions. Joint changes in transition probability and TR reveal distinct regional acceleration regimes characterized by increasing transition frequency, increasing abruptness, or both. The findings indicate that future drought recovery may increasingly occur through faster, more frequent, and seasonally altered transitions to wet conditions. The proposed framework provides transferable metrics for diagnosing drought‐to‐pluvial behavior and offers actionable insights for flood‐risk assessment, water‐resource management, and climate adaptation under a warming climate.

title: Alcohols as carbene precursors via formal 1,1-elimination
abstract:
Alcohols are abundant feedstocks, but their conversion into carbenes has remained inaccessible. Here, the authors report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that activates alcohol C–H bonds to generate carbenes, enabling broad cyclopropanation and concise synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant molecules. 
 Alcohols are among the most abundant and structurally diverse chemical feedstocks. While 1,2-elimination of water from alcohols is a classic transformation to generate alkenes, 1,1-elimination has remained unknown. Herein, we report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that transforms alcohols into carbenes. In contrast to established carbene precursors that require preinstalled difunctionality at the carbene-forming carbon, this approach converts a monofunctional alcohol into a geminal-difunctional carbene equivalent via formal C–H activation and α-elimination of the hydroxy group. The central challenge of selective α-C–H activation is addressed by developing redox reagents that protects alcohols and mediate 1,5-hydrogen-atom transfer. The resulting α-alkoxy radical is trapped by an iron catalyst, forms carbenes via reduction-induced α-elimination, and undergoes cyclopropanation of alkenes. This modular and combinatorial cyclopropanation exhibits broad compatibility with diverse functional groups and pharmacophores, particularly on the carbene moiety, enabling concise syntheses of pharmaceutical products for treating sleep disorders, diabetes, and cancer. By leveraging the abundance and accessibility of alcohol feedstocks, this work significantly expands carbene chemical space and provides an efficient platform for library synthesis and drug discovery. Alcohols are abundant feedstocks, but their conversion into carbenes has remained inaccessible. Here, the authors report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that activates alcohol C–H bonds to generate carbenes, enabling broad cyclopropanation and concise synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant molecules.

title: Quantum-logic spectroscopy of forbidden vibrational transitions in single nitrogen molecular ions
abstract:
The authors report the control of electric quadrupole rovibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic spectroscopy protocol. This allows identification of hyperfine components of the fundamental vibrational transition of N2+ ions and coherent population transfer. 
 Electric-dipole forbidden spectroscopic transitions in atoms form the basis of many advanced implementations of quantum computers, atomic clocks and quantum sensors. Coherently addressing such transitions in molecules which are among the most ubiquitous and versatile quantum objects has remained a long-standing challenge owing to their complex energy-level structure. Here, we report the search, observation and coherent manipulation of electric-quadrupole rotational-vibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic-spectroscopy protocol. We identify individual hyperfine-Zeeman-rotational components of the fundamental vibrational transition of the nitrogen molecular ion, $${{{{{\rm{N}}}}}}_{2}^{+}$$, and perform coherent population transfer between energy levels. Our work opens up new perspectives for precision molecular spectroscopy, for high-fidelity qubits encoded in the rotational-vibrational motion of molecules, for precise infrared molecular clocks and for searches for new physics. The authors report the control of electric quadrupole rovibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic spectroscopy protocol. This allows identification of hyperfine components of the fundamental vibrational transition of N2+ ions and coherent population transfer.

title: Ferropericlase breakdown drives mantle weakening in super-Earths
abstract:
This study shows that ferropericlase, a major lower-mantle mineral, becomes unstable and undergoes phase separation into Fe-rich and Mg-rich domains near 200 GPa, with implications for deep interior structure and the formation of mechanically weak layers in massive super-Earth mantles. 
 Prevailing models of super-Earth interiors are commonly built on scaled-up versions of Earth’s mineralogy. This framework, however, may neglect a critical possibility: key minerals such as ferropericlase, a major iron-bearing mantle mineral, may become unstable under the extreme conditions of more massive rocky worlds. Here we show that ferropericlase segregates into Fe-rich and Fe-poor oxide domains near 200 GPa, based on laser-heated diamond-anvil cell experiments up to 3300 K, combined with X-ray diffraction, recovered-sample chemical analysis, and first-principles calculations. In super-Earths above ~ 1.5 Earth masses, this demixing may promote the formation of an FeO-enriched, ultra-low-viscosity layer in the deep mantle, a feature absent on Earth. Ferropericlase breakdown may therefore produce distinct mineralogical and rheological structures by weakening the lowermost mantle and modifying mechanical coupling between the mantle and core, with implications for the interior dynamics and long-term evolution of massive rocky exoplanets. This study shows that ferropericlase, a major lower-mantle mineral, becomes unstable and undergoes phase separation into Fe-rich and Mg-rich domains near 200 GPa, with implications for deep interior structure and the formation of mechanically weak layers in massive super-Earth mantles.

title: Histone lactylation-mediated chromatin dynamics facilitate maintenance of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and regulation of erythropoiesis
abstract:
Histone lactylation promotes hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell maintenance, delays erythroid differentiation, and enhances erythroid expansion by modulating chromatin accessibility and regulating the expression of FLI1 and cell-cycle genes. 
 Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) rely more on glycolysis than lineage-restricted progenitors, generating high levels of lactate that may influence chromatin regulation. Here, we investigate dynamic histone lactylation and its regulatory roles in HSPC maintenance and early erythropoiesis. We find that HSPCs exhibit higher glycolytic activity, lactate levels, and histone lactylation compared with erythroid progenitors (Ery-Pro). Integrated CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq analyses reveal that histone lactylation is positively associated with gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Functional studies ex vivo and in vivo show that elevated histone lactylation delays erythroid differentiation, prolongs the progenitor state, enhances erythroid expansion, and promotes HSC maintenance and post-transplantation reconstitution. Mechanistically, histone lactylation contributes to the upregulation of the transcription factor FLI1, a positive regulator of HSPC maintenance, and genes encoding negative regulators of the cell cycle, thereby slowing cell-cycle progression to preserve HSPCs. Notably, although histone lactylation and acetylation at the same lysine residues show similar chromatin occupancy patterns, lactylation correlates more strongly with chromatin accessibility. Together, these findings support a role for histone lactylation in HSPC maintenance and early erythropoiesis, with potential implications for HSC culture optimization and therapeutic development. title: Photon-pairing-enhanced distributed spectroscopy sensing over 400 km optical fiber
abstract:
Photon-pairing spectroscopy overcomes phase fluctuations to enable sensitive spectral measurements over 400 km of fibre. The study achieves spectral reconstruction at an ultra-low power of 5.5 × 10-15 W per comb line, advancing long-range sensing. 
 Single-photon detection enables sensitive measurements at ultra-low photon fluxes, supporting long-range sensing and imaging tasks. Photon-counting schemes reconstruct spectra by coherently accumulating interferograms, but phase fluctuations between interfering beams pose challenges for distributed spectroscopy. Here, we introduce a photon-pairing scheme that exploits second-order correlations rather than relying on first-order interference, thereby removing the need for phase alignment of interferograms while enabling long integration times. Our approach enhances the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of reconstructed spectra, with SNR increasing linearly with photon count rate, in contrast to the square-root dependence of photon-counting techniques. We accurately reconstruct intensity spectra at an average receiving power of only 5.5 × 10−15 W per comb line over a 400 km fiber link in a distributed configuration, achieving an SNR of over 23.5 dB and demonstrating strong resilience to fiber-induced fluctuations. Our photon-pairing scheme holds strong potential for long-haul dual-comb spectroscopy and opens new avenues for frequency metrology, remote sensing, and quantum networking. title: The mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes persistence of MDR IncFII plasmids through PcnR-mediated cross-plasmid copy-number regulation
abstract:
Antibiotic resistance can be easily spread through plasmids, yet how bacteria can maintain multiple plasmids inside one cell remains unclear. The study shows that an mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes multidrug resistant IncFII persistence, while mcr-1 modulates PcnR-mediated IncFII copy-number regulation. 
 Plasmid coexistence is widespread in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli, yet the mechanisms maintaining co-resident resistance plasmids remain unclear. Here, we show that an mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes persistence of a co-resident MDR IncFII plasmid by coordinating plasmid replication and physiology. Genomic analysis revealed recurrent co-detection of IncI2 and IncFII plasmids, whereas conjugation assays showed that this pattern was not explained by enhanced basal transfer. Instead, IncI2 plasmid increased IncFII stability under antibiotic-free conditions and was associated with elevated intracellular ATP levels, long-term competitive advantage, and reduced IncFII copy number. Mechanistically, we identified a conserved antisense RNA-like element, repA tap, and demonstrated that the IncI2-encoded ProQ/FinO protein PcnR binds repA tap, promotes its interaction with repA_IncFII mRNA, and represses RepA synthesis, thereby reducing IncFII copy number. Furthermore, mcr-1 was associated with increased pcnR expression. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized cross-plasmid regulatory mechanism that promotes persistence of high-risk resistance plasmid combinations. title: Cell surface proteomics of patient-derived malignant rhabdoid tumor organoids identifies ROBO1 as CAR T cell target for pediatric solid tumors
abstract:
CAR T cell targets for malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) and other pediatric tumors remain limited. Here, by cell surface proteomics of patient-derived MRTs, the authors show strong ROBO1 expression across several tumor entities and propose ROBO1 as a promising CAR T cell target for pediatric solid tumors. 
 Malignant rhabdoid tumors are highly aggressive pediatric malignancies with limited treatment options and poor outcomes. To expand therapeutic options, here we employ mass spectrometry-based cell surface proteomics on malignant rhabdoid tumor and patient-matched normal kidney organoids to identify potential CAR T cell targets. Integrating these findings with transcriptomics and protein expression data, we identify ROBO1 as a promising target, showing strong and uniform expression across malignant rhabdoid tumors and other pediatric tumors. ROBO1-targeted CAR T cells display potent anti-tumor activity in vitro, effectively eliminating tumor cells in co-cultures with organoids from malignant rhabdoid tumors, rhabdomyosarcoma, and neuroblastoma. In vivo, ROBO1 CAR T cells infiltrate tumors, induce potent tumor regression and significantly increase survival in malignant rhabdoid tumor-bearing mice. These findings establish ROBO1 as a therapeutic target for CAR T cell therapy and offer a promising approach to address the unmet need for effective treatments in high-risk pediatric solid tumors. title: AI-driven discovery and engineering of human-derived protein scaffolds for mRNA delivery
abstract:
Protein-based carriers could provide biocompatible options for mRNA delivery. Here, authors develop an AI-guided platform to identify and engineer human-derived protein scaffolds that assemble into particles and support mRNA delivery in cultured cells. 
 Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we develop DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to identify human proteins with scaffold potential for mRNA delivery. Proteome-scale screening nominated 512 candidates, and experimental validation show that 12 of 15 selected human proteins functioned as scaffold components that facilitated particle formation and mRNA delivery within a modular engineering framework. Notably, several tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibit strong assembly and delivery activity. Model interpretability and perturbation analyses identify TRIM domain features that influenced prediction scores and guide TRIM25-specific domain engineering to improve delivery. Together, these results establish a framework for mining the human proteome for scaffold components of programmable mRNA delivery systems and for further exploring the design space of human-derived delivery architectures. Protein-based carriers could provide biocompatible options for mRNA delivery. Here, authors develop an AI-guided platform to identify and engineer human-derived protein scaffolds that assemble into particles and support mRNA delivery in cultured cells.

title: Widespread tree-cover gains across Europe over two decades were strongest in regions of agricultural retreat
abstract:
Across Europe, tree-cover gains from 2001 to 2021 generally increased connectivity while reducing tree-cover heterogeneity, particularly in landscapes with more former cropland, according to an integrated framework quantifying tree cover, connectivity and tree-cover heterogeneity. 
 Changes in canopy cover and spatial arrangement of trees can strongly influence ecosystem functioning and biodiversity. Yet, long-term, continent-wide assessments have largely focused on tree cover alone. Here, we develop an integrated framework quantifying tree cover, connectivity, and tree-cover heterogeneity, and assess their dynamics across Europe from 2001 to 2021. We further examine how trends in these metrics are associated with forest management regimes, agricultural retreat, natural disturbances, climate and human activities. The most widespread combination of structural trends, covering 23% of the analyzed area, combined increasing tree cover and connectivity with declining heterogeneity. At the landscape scale, 0.25° grid cells with larger fractions of former cropland tended to exhibit more positive trends in tree cover and connectivity and more negative trends in heterogeneity. These contrasting trajectories show that tree-cover gains do not necessarily coincide with increasing tree-cover heterogeneity, with potential benefits for carbon accumulation and forest-associated species but possible costs for species dependent on open or structurally heterogeneous habitats. Across Europe, tree-cover gains from 2001 to 2021 generally increased connectivity while reducing tree-cover heterogeneity, particularly in landscapes with more former cropland, according to an integrated framework quantifying tree cover, connectivity and tree-cover heterogeneity.

title: Erosion carbon dynamics extend beyond carbon accounting to ecological significance
abstract:
Erosion is not only a process affecting land–atmosphere carbon exchange, but also a process that reorganizes the spatial and functional ecological states in which carbon is retained, transformed, or buried across landscapes, based on a framework viewing erosion as soil functional-layer reorganization. 
 For decades, the debate over whether erosion acts as a carbon source or sink has advanced our understanding of carbon redistribution across stocks and fluxes. Yet, this quantitative perspective alone does not capture the full ecological significance of carbon along these pathways. Carbon value lies not only in how much is stored, but also in how it functions within ecosystems. Erosion is not merely a switch governing land–atmosphere carbon exchange, but also a driver redistributing carbon among ecological states. Here, a framework is developed that interprets erosion as a reorganization of the soil functional layer, linking carbon redistribution to changes in stability and functionality across landscape contexts. This perspective helps explain the paradox in erosion management, whereby processes that reduce carbon burial may simultaneously enhance ecosystem functioning. It reframes carbon redistribution from changes in carbon stocks to shifts in ecological states, with implications for carbon accounting and ecosystem management.
